Fix a finite integer $n\ge1$ and a dispersion value $\phi$. For each $1\le i\le n$, let $\mathcal Y_i\subseteq\mathbb R$ carry its Borel sigma algebra and let $\nu_i$ be a sigma-finite positive measure on it. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $b:J\to\mathbb R$ be twice continuously differentiable, let $a_i(\phi)>0$, and let $c_i(\,\cdot\,,\phi)$ be measurable. An **explicit one-parameter exponential-family response contract** supplies, for each $\theta_i\in J$, a density or mass function relative to $\nu_i$,

$$f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

The contract requires $f_i\ge0$, $\int f_i(\,\cdot\,;\theta_i,\phi)\,d\nu_i=1$ for every $\theta_i\in J$, and a fixed support $S_i\in\mathcal A_i$ such that $f_i>0$ on $S_i$ and $f_i=0$ off $S_i$, up to a $\nu_i$-null set independent of $\theta_i$. When the mean and variance identities are used, it also requires a finite second moment and locally uniform integrable envelopes for the first and second $\theta_i$ derivatives of $f_i$ on $S_i$.

For a vector $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\in J^n$, the **product sampling law** is the finite product $\bigotimes_{i=1}^n P_{i,\theta_i,\phi}$, where $P_{i,\theta_i,\phi}$ has density $f_i$ relative to $\nu_i$. The coordinate responses are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Their product base measure is $\nu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\nu_i$ on $\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal A_i$. The next lemma verifies that the joint density is $\prod_i f_i$.

Every scientific application also records a [[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]: it names the observation space and record, scientific and analysis units, index meanings, response and predictor maps, target, observation mechanism, support, law, conditioning, and adequacy assumptions. The contract does not itself imply independence or common support; those are explicit hypotheses of this response-family definition. Here $i$ is only a component index until the application assigns it a scientific unit or time meaning.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

$$q_\theta(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$$

relative to $\nu$. At any $y$ for which every factor $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$ is positive, the log likelihood is $\log q_\theta(y)=\sum_i\log f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for

The mean value theorem [F2] applied to $q'$ makes $q'$ strictly decreasing. For any $0<t<1$, another application of [F2] gives $(q(t)-q(0))/t=q'(u)$ for some $u\in(0,t)$ and $(q(1)-q(t))/(1-t)=q'(v)$ for some $v\in(t,1)$; strict decrease gives the first secant slope larger than the second, which rearranges to $q(t)>(1-t)q(0)+tq(1)$. Two distinct stationary points would give $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$ on their connecting segment, contradicting strict decrease. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

$$\ell(\beta;y,\phi)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

For a differentiable log likelihood, the **score** is $U(\beta;y,\phi):=\nabla_\beta\ell(\beta;y,\phi)$. When its entries have finite second moments, the **expected score outer-product information** is $I(\beta,\phi):=\mathbb E_{\beta,\phi}[U U^\mathsf T]$. This page treats $X$ as fixed or conditions on its realized value; it supplies no random-design asymptotic conclusion.

Fix a finite integer $n\ge1$ and a dispersion value $\phi$. For each $1\le i\le n$, let $\mathcal Y_i\subseteq\mathbb R$ carry its Borel sigma algebra and let $\nu_i$ be a sigma-finite positive measure on it. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $b:J\to\mathbb R$ be twice continuously differentiable, let $a_i(\phi)>0$, and let $c_i(\,\cdot\,,\phi)$ be measurable. An **explicit one-parameter exponential-family response contract** supplies, for each $\theta_i\in J$, a density or mass function relative to $\nu_i$,

$$f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}+c_i(y_i,\phi)\right\}.$$

The contract requires $f_i\ge0$, $\int f_i(\,\cdot\,;\theta_i,\phi)\,d\nu_i=1$ for every $\theta_i\in J$, and a fixed support $S_i\in\mathcal A_i$ such that $f_i>0$ on $S_i$ and $f_i=0$ off $S_i$, up to a $\nu_i$-null set independent of $\theta_i$. When the mean and variance identities are used, it also requires a finite second moment and locally uniform integrable envelopes for the first and second $\theta_i$ derivatives of $f_i$ on $S_i$.

For a vector $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\in J^n$, the **product sampling law** is the finite product $\bigotimes_{i=1}^n P_{i,\theta_i,\phi}$, where $P_{i,\theta_i,\phi}$ has density $f_i$ relative to $\nu_i$. Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor

2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable

Assume each $\eta_i\mapsto\theta_i$ is differentiable, each $\eta_i\mapsto\mu_i$ is differentiable with $\dot\mu_i:=d\mu_i/d\eta_i\ne0$, $V_i:=b''(\theta_i)>0$, the component scores have finite second moments, and the common-support, differentiability, and local integrable derivative-envelope conditions from [[def-glm-observation-family]] hold. Put

$$w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i},\qquad z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i}.$$

For every observed $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for each $i$, the score and expected score outer-product information are

$$U(\beta;y,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\left(\frac{\dot\mu_i(y_i-\mu_i)}{a(\phi)V_i}\right)_{i=1}^n,\qquad I(\beta,\phi)=X^\mathsf T\operatorname{diag}(w_i)X.$$

In particular, if $X$ has full column rank, then $I$ is positive definite.

Inputs are an observed response vector $y$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, a finite design matrix $X$, an admissible finite current parameter $\beta$, and a GLM with common scale $a(\phi)>0$. Require each $\dot\mu_i=d\mu_i/d\eta_i$ to be finite and nonzero and each $V_i=b''(\theta_i)$ to be finite and positive.

1. Compute $\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta$ and $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$.
2. Compute the **working response** and positive weight
$$z_i=\eta_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\dot\mu_i},\qquad w_i=\frac{\dot\mu_i^2}{a(\phi)V_i}.$$
3. Form $W^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$ using [[thm-of-square-roots]], and put $A=W^{1/2}X$, $r=W^{1/2}z$. By [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]] and [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]], form $A^+$. Return $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=A^+r$, the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm member of the nonempty weighted least-squares minimizer set by [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]].

The Moore--Penrose convention makes the procedure single-valued even when $X$ is rank deficient; the underlying least-squares minimizer need not then be unique. Existence and the minimum-norm property follow from [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]] and [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]. Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge1$, a finite design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with rows $x_i^\mathsf T$, a dispersion value $\phi$, and an open parameter domain $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. A **generalized linear model (GLM)** on this design consists of the response family in [[def-glm-observation-family]], a differentiable one-to-one link $g:\mathcal M\to g(\mathcal M)$ on a specified mean domain $\mathcal M$, and a specified map $\tau:\mathcal M\to J$ satisfying $b'(\tau(\mu))=\mu$. For $\beta\in\Theta$, put

$$\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i),\qquad \theta_i=\tau(\mu_i),$$

and require $\eta_i\in g(\mathcal M)$ and $\theta_i\in J$ for every $i$. The **canonical link** is the choice $g=\tau$, equivalently $\theta_i=\eta_i$. When $\theta_i=\eta_i$ and the component scales are common, write $a_i(\phi)=a(\phi)>0$; this common-scale restriction is part of every formula that uses $a(\phi)$.

The joint sampling density is the product density from [[lem-glm-product-density]]. For an observed $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ with $f_i(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)>0$ for every $i$, define its log likelihood by

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let

a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

derivations.claim: Each predictor is a finite sum of products of real design and parameter entries, and each mean is a unique finite real value by [F2]. The observed response coordinates are finite real numbers by [F1]. Thus $z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)/\dot\mu_i$ is finite and uniquely determined because its denominator is nonzero. Likewise $w_i=\dot\mu_i^2/(a(\phi)V_i)$ is finite and strictly positive: its numerator is positive and its denominator is a finite positive real number. These operations refer to real arithmetic, with no floating-point overflow assertion.

By [F3] each $w_i$ has one finite positive square root. Consequently the diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w_i})$, the weighted design $A=DX$, and the target $r=Dz$ are unique finite real matrices or vectors with the specified dimensions. By [F4] the $p\times n$ matrix $A^+$ exists uniquely for every rank of $A$, so the returned $A^+r$ exists uniquely in $\mathbb R^p$. No inverse of $X^\mathsf T W X$ was required at this stage.

For every $\gamma\in\mathbb R^p$, the diagonal construction gives $\|A\gamma-r\|_2^2=\sum_iw_i(x_i^\mathsf T\gamma-z_i)^2$. Since a nonnegative real number and its square have the same minimizing arguments, [F5] makes $A^+r$ a member of the displayed weighted least-squares minimizer set and the unique member of minimum Euclidean norm. In particular that set is nonempty even when $X$ is rank deficient. The minimum-norm property is the conclusion of the supplied theorem, not an extra condition imposed on the algorithm's inputs.

The weighted normal matrix is symmetric, and for every $u\in\mathbb R^p$ one has $u^\mathsf T H u=\sum_iw_i(x_i^\mathsf T u)^2=\|Au\|_2^2\ge0$, so $H$ is positive semidefinite. If $Xu=0$, then $Hu=X^\mathsf T W Xu=0$. Conversely, if $Hu=0$, the displayed sum is zero, and its finitely many nonnegative terms with strictly positive $w_i$ force every $x_i^\mathsf T u=0$; hence $Xu=0$. This proves $\ker H=\ker X$. Steps 2.1–3.1 apply equally when this kernel is nontrivial.

If $X=0$, then $A=0$. The zero matrix satisfies the Penrose equations, so uniqueness in [F4] gives $A^+=0$ and the algorithm returns $0$. The weighted objective is then constant in $\gamma$, so every vector is a minimizer and $0$ is its unique minimum-norm member, consistent with step 3.1. A single response, zero observed responses, and other ranks use the same proof whenever the original admissibility conditions hold. Thus all stated well-definedness claims hold without an invertibility condition or a condition that the returned vector remain in the model domain.
